publications.title: Humanity's Last Exam
publications.subtitle: Center for AI Safety
publications.description: Contributions: Data AuditorBenchmarks are important tools for tracking the rapid advancements in large language model (LLM) capabilities. However, benchmarks are not keeping pace in difficulty: LLMs now achieve over 90\% accuracy on popular benchmarks like MMLU, limiting informed measurement of state-of-the-art LLM capabilities. In response, we introduce Humanity's Last Exam (HLE), a multi-modal benchmark at the frontier of human knowledge, designed to be the final closed-ended academic benchmark of its kind with broad subject coverage. HLE consists of 2,500 questions across dozens of subjects, including mathematics, humanities, and the natural sciences. HLE is developed globally by subject-matter experts and consists of multiple-choice and short-answer questions suitable for automated grading. Each question has a known solution that is unambiguous and easily verifiable, but cannot be quickly answered via internet retrieval. State-of-the-art LLMs demonstrate low accuracy and calibration on HLE, highlighting a significant gap between current LLM capabilities and the expert human frontier on closed-ended academic questions. To inform research and policymaking upon a clear understanding of model capabilities, we publicly release HLE at this https URL.

projects.title: HackUTD X - Winner
projects.description: HomeReady Pro offers a multifaceted set of functionalities to users, including:Financial Eligibility Assessment: Users can input their financial data, including credit score, income, monthly expenses, and other relevant variables. The application then employs a complex algorithm to evaluate their eligibility for their desired homeownership.Data Analysis: The app conducts an in-depth analysis of user data, looking for patterns and trends that affect homeownership eligibility. This analysis provides valuable insights into which financial variables are most likely to impact a user's eligibility. This feature is crucial for users who wish to understand common obstacles to homeownership.Customized Recommendations: Based on the analysis and the user's eligibility status, the app generates personalized recommendations. The app provides unique tips and suggestions to improve their financial situation for future homeownership.Winner of Best Use of Kintone at HackUTD X

projects.title: AIFAHacks - Winner
projects.description: PaveGuard is a user-friendly mobile app that revolutionizes pothole reporting. Users can instantly scan potholes which are then uploaded to a database. Our trained model then classifies the images by obstruction type (pothole, fallen tree, crack, etc) and then uploads the images and the user provided data and geodata to an admin console. City officials can then log in and access these images, where they can then take action on these potholes in a much more proficient manner. This reduces the $3 billion spent annually by drivers on pothole-related damages, which could be much better used in America's growing cities to address social issues.Winner of 3rd Place Overall at AIFAHacks - AI Hackathon For Social Good

We went to Stanford University and won Google’s AI track at TreeHacks 🏆 This weekend, my team, Spandan Patel , Ekagra Gupta , and I built Clarifyd, a classroom support tool for students with disabilities. Our goal? Provide teachers and students with immediate help, without waiting through lengthy school licensing and accommodations workflows. But honestly, the win was a small part of it. TreeHacks was unreal. 1,098 participants and $606,605 in cash on the line. Sam Altman, Garry Tan, and Ali Partovi opened, and afterwards it was straight to building. We pulled an all-nighter, took a 1am poker break to reset our brains, then went right back to debugging before demos and judging. And somehow, everything came together at the end. I did all of it on basically no sleep. Left Chicago at 3am for my flight out, got back at 7am, then had a midterm that afternoon. Worth it. Big thanks to Benedict (couldn’t find your LinkedIn), Michelle Vinocour , Anson Omar , and the whole TreeHacks team for running a great event and taking care of everyone all weekend! On to the next one 🚀 #Stanford #Treehacks #Google #Hackathon ...more ...more

Wrapped up TreeHacks this past weekend and... we won! Our team placed 2nd in the Cloud AI Track sponsored by Google . After 36 hours of coming up with the perfect idea and executing, I'm glad to have walked away from this amazing event with a win. Our team built Clarifyd, a real-time lecture platform where students watch AI-generated videos, compete on quiz leaderboards, and get instant answers — all while the lecture is happening. It was surreal to see big names in tech like Sam Altman and Garry Tan in person, speaking openly about their experiences. I also want to give a massive shout-out to the team at Google that showed up, including Benedict and Vivian , and other sponsors I was able to talk to, including Amanda Yiu and Grace Gong . Also, thank you to the organizing team that coordinated such an amazing event. Finally, I can't thank my team members, Daryl Echeazu and Ekagra Gupta , enough for locking in with me to pull off this win. (p.s. I had to recreate the project announcement picture because we were too excited to take it in time) #TreeHacks #Google #Stanford ...more

It's official. I'm staying a Denver Nugget. Plot twist. Yes, I signed an offer sheet with Oklahoma City and yes, Denver matched it. I know some people are confused, and some fans are even upset. How could I sign with a rival? I get it. But I also need people to understand something. This is a business. Front offices treat it that way every day and players have to do the same. I went into free agency with clear priorities: a team that fits my skillset, a championship culture, and an organization I believe in. Both Denver and OKC checked those boxes. Either way, I was landing somewhere that made sense. The offer sheet was a business decision. It ensured I ended up in the right situation w/ what I felt was the right compensation regardless of what happened next. And along the way, I made a little history. The largest fully guaranteed offer sheet ever signed by an undrafted player converted from a two-way contract. From a two-way with no safety net to this. I don't take that lightly. Now I get to keep building with the team that bet on me from the start. Back to work!

Last Saturday, I served as a host and judge for Ramp 's largest-ever external hackathon. Months ago, I reached out to Richard Noguchi to see if a Codex sponsorship for a Ramp hackathon would be possible. Months of back and forth helped us prepare all the logistics for the hackathon. I’m here to share the top 3 winners in the Codex prize track. 🥇 Relay, by Ryan Amiri , Aadi Biyani , and Kile H. Relay built custom “adapters” for Codex to use Desktop Apps. It made Codex play Minecraft PVPs, and nobody beat the AI. 🥈 Spex, by Sofia Bodnar , Chris Chang , Armaan Agrawal , and Santosh S. Spex built a custom model to predict Codex tool calls + events. Benchmarked against vanilla Codex and offered significant latency improvement. 🥉 Governor, by Aarav Raina , Aryan Sharma , Azdeen Zack , and Thomas Ou Governor deployed an AI token spend management system inside of VSCode’s extension marketplace + a router to set spend limits on existing token spend. Thanks to everyone who competed! Picking the winners was not an easy decision at all. A special shoutout to Sandra Yang , Satyam Singh , Richard Noguchi , Angela Wu , Katherine W. , and Cat Choy for organizing, judging, and supporting the event! PS: I’m currently working on a longer-form article to break down the behind the scenes of developing the hackathon's software. Stay tuned. :)

After four unforgettable years, I’m grateful to share that I’ve graduated from UCLA with a B.S. in Computer Science. 🎓 I’m also honored to have received the Engineering Achievement Award in Student Welfare, which recognizes students who have made outstanding contributions to student welfare and service to the campus community. Looking back, some of my most memorable college experiences came from saying yes to opportunities I never could have predicted. One of the most fulfilling parts of my experience was helping organize LA Hacks . I had the opportunity to work with an incredible team to grow the event, reach thousands of students, partner with dozens of sponsors, and break several organization records along the way. It became one of my biggest professional experiences in college teaching me how to lead an organization, manage large-scale logistics and budgeting, and coordinate across multiple stakeholders under pressure. Helping LA Hacks be recognized as UCLA Engineering’s Most Grown Student Organization of 2026 was an honor, but what I’m most proud of is the community we built and the impact we created together. 💻 The UCLA Association of Chinese Americans also became one of the most meaningful communities I was part of, in ways I didn’t expect. While I’m grateful for the professional side of networking with sponsors and creating opportunities for members of the Chinese community, what stood out most were the friendships, mentorship, and belonging that came from it. Helping coordinate one of ACA’s largest intern classes, watching new members find their place, and forming so many meaningful connections helped make a big school like UCLA feel closer. 🤝 Playing drums with the UCLA Marching Band was another unforgettable part of my time in college. It allowed me to continue pursuing a hobby I’ve always loved at a higher level while sharing that passion through performances for others. Through the band, I had the privilege of performing across the country and even in Taiwan, represent UCLA at gigs throughout LA, and accidentally create some funny social media content along the way that reached far more people than I ever expected. 🥁 Looking back, the moments I’ll remember most aren’t just the big milestones, but the late nights, spontaneous adventures, long trips, and people who made UCLA feel like home. I came to school with the intent to only focus on academics and get a good job, but I’m leaving with a much greater appreciation for everything outside the classroom: the people you surround yourself with, the opportunities you say yes to, and the unexpected moments that teach you how to grow. Thank you to my family, friends, mentors and everyone who supported me along the way. I wouldn’t be where I am today without you. I’m excited to begin my next chapter as a Software Engineer at Anduril Industries in Costa Mesa this August. 🚀 I'm grateful for everything this chapter gave me, and I'm excited for what comes next. Go Bruins! 🐻

I’m thrilled to announce that I’ve joined Coinbase as the Chief Information Security Officer (CISO)! My career has focused on advising security teams on emerging threats, building security products, and supporting organizations through high-stakes incident response. As the threat landscape evolves toward increasingly complex, decentralized ecosystems with AI-enabled attackers, it’s time to step out of the advisory seat and take on this challenge directly. I’m honored to join Jeff Lunglhofer and the exceptional team at Coinbase. Together, we will secure the future of financial services, disrupt threat actors, and scale a highly resilient world-class security architecture. Incredibly excited for this next chapter. Let’s go!

My first six months at UCLA were lonely. It was my first time living away from home, and I was surrounded by amazing people but couldn't seem to actually connect with any of them. I called my mom Vera Shokina every day, and she drove down from the Bay whenever she could. What I didn't know yet was that I'd already met most of the people this post is about: the ones I'd end up pulling all-nighters with, trading secrets with, and, four years later, calling my closest friends. It was just a matter for spending some more time with them. In honors calculus, I trauma-bonded with Yutian Yang (who would become my roommate for the next three years!), Julia Gu , Kuan Qian , and Karley Tioran . My next-door neighbors Hannah Kendall and Annie Feng , plus their friend Abigail Chang , became a weekly breakfast club where we'd debrief the week. Joy Cheng was one of the first people I met as a move-in assistant, and I met Surya Subbarao at a math competition (which he ended up winning!). I thought I was meeting them in passing, but four years later they're some of my best friends. When I showed up to my first LA Hacks meeting, I was disappointed to learn it was for organizing the hackathon, not competing in it. I was too embarrassed to leave. So I sat through it, realized what an incredible group of people it was, and ended up finding my biggest group of friends: Shubham Kumar , Claire Chien , Priyanshu Sharma , Anagha Srivatsav , Allison Huang , Zoey Ho , Sean Chan, Isabella Qian , Arya Bhalla , Armaan Bassi , Julie Cover , Anooshkha Shetty , Asmi K. , Sonav Agarwal , John Connell , and Tom Binford . Shubham, Sonav, John, and Tom became my go-to hackathon teammates once I started competing myself. They’ve seen me at rock bottom when I lose all hope for our project at 4am, and then in a giggle fit 5 minutes later going delirious from the sleep deprivation. I joined club track and met two of my closest friends today, Evan Leach and Nick Pavlosky . Something about feeling like you’re about to pass out after a 400 gets you really close, I guess! I bonded with Rory Hemmings, Amanda W , and Sam Gerstmann while interning in New York, and kept in touch with them once we were back at UCLA because I have the best conversations with them. I ran into Nyla Zia during a UCLA event she was organizing, and we hit it off immediately and started getting coffee together regularly. And I met with Maxine Wu, Alina Susu , Peter Nguyen , Joyce Chen , and Eric Wang through mutual friends in passing, but ended up bonding with them more deeply. To all of you, and the many others I bumped into along the way, thank you. You made me who I am now, and created memories I’ll look back at fondly for the rest of my life. UCLA, I’ll miss you!

Winning an NBA Championship with the New York Knicks is everything I ever dreamed of. The fans, the city, this organization… This is why I came to New York. I’m so proud of this team. No matter the situation, we never stopped believing in each other or lost sight of our goal. With enough work and enough belief, your dreams are possible and you can overcome any obstacle. Whatever it is in life, believe that you belong. People might disagree but let that strengthen your belief because with hard work, preparation, and the right mindset, anything is possible. I can't wait to celebrate with my family, my teammates, the city of New York, and everyone who's been here from day one. We don’t win this championship without you! I also look forward to continuing to support other people's dreams through my work with the Second Round Foundation , where our mission is helping young people determine their own success no matter where they come from. It is important to me to support the under-resourced, under-represented, and under-estimated, and to ensure that they have the tools, guidance, and belief they need to achieve their dreams. Thank you, New York. I am forever grateful. And always remember…The Magic is in the Work. - JB
